summary:
An operator-focused guide from Allwork.space, written by a consultant who builds CRMs and lead management systems for coworking operators, mapping the three primary lead channels for flexible workspace: organic, brokers/tenant reps, and marketplaces/lead gen platforms. The framing problem is capacity: in most coworking spaces the person answering leads is also doing community building, hospitality, member care, coffee and tours, so time spent on one channel is taken from another.

Organic covers the operator website (SEO, content, keywords) and the Google Business Profile. The author argues the profile is underinvested relative to the website, often appearing ahead of regular search results in local and map searches, and suggests operators compare profile metrics against website analytics, predicting the profile drives many times more leads. Many profiles have no products listed and unfilled sections; the author recommends assigning weekly ownership of profile content.

Commercial real estate brokers and tenant reps mainly bring enterprise requirements and suit operators with substantial private office inventory or strong landlord relationships; smaller local spaces likely will not work with brokers. Kane Willmott, CEO of IQ Offices, is cited as running a resourced broker program that generates most of his leads, more than paid ads. Some brokers blast one requirement to every space in a market, making speed of response decisive; other losses are simply inventory fit. These platforms also generate many dead leads.

Marketplaces and lead gen platforms (sometimes called online brokers, distinct from tenant reps) are third-party digital marketers matching inventory to demand. Enterprises want one master service agreement rather than contracting with many operators or having staff expense meeting rooms. Regus, WeWork and Industrious can sign directly; independents reach that demand via listings. Inventory-to-platform matching: day passes and hot desks to Deskpass; meeting rooms and offices to LiquidSpace and Gable; enterprise-licensed offices to Upsuite, Desana, LiquidSpace, Gable, Preferred Office Network; event space to Peerspace and Giggster. Enterprise demand includes smaller companies, not only Fortune 500.

claims.claim: Google Business Profiles typically generate many times more leads for coworking operators than their websites
claims.stat: many times the number of leads
claims.attribution: Article author (coworking lead generation consultant, Allwork.space)

claims.claim: IQ Offices gets most of its leads from brokers rather than from paid advertising
claims.attribution: Article author, describing Kane Willmott, CEO of IQ Offices

claims.claim: Brokers sometimes push a single requirement to every coworking space on their platform in a market, so the operator who responds first often wins
Enterprises prefer a single master service agreement and one booking platform rather than contracting with operators in each market or having employees expense meeting rooms
claims.stat: a company with people in a hundred markets would not contract with a hundred operators

claims.claim: Regus, WeWork and Industrious can sign enterprise agreements directly, while most independent operators reach that demand through marketplace listings
Local remote workers booking meeting rooms often lack booking authority and must use the employer's chosen platform
